search_paper_list.title: Scaling Laws of Synthetic Images for Model Training ... for Now
search_paper_list.summary:
Recent significant advances in text-to-image models unlock the possibility of
training vision systems using synthetic images, potentially overcoming the
difficulty of collecting curated data at scale. It is unclear, however, how
these models behave at scale, as more synthetic data is added to the training
set. In this paper we study the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by
state of the art text-to-image models, for the training of supervised models:
image classifiers with label supervision, and CLIP with language supervision.
We identify several factors, including text prompts, classifier-free guidance
scale, and types of text-to-image models, that significantly affect scaling
behavior. After tuning these factors, we observe that synthetic images
demonstrate a scaling trend similar to, but slightly less effective than, real
images in CLIP training, while they significantly underperform in scaling when
training supervised image classifiers. Our analysis indicates that the main
reason for this underperformance is the inability of off-the-shelf
text-to-image models to generate certain concepts, a limitation that
significantly impairs the training of image classifiers. Our findings also
suggest that scaling synthetic data can be particularly effective in scenarios
such as: (1) when there is a limited supply of real images for a supervised
problem (e.g., fewer than 0.5 million images in ImageNet), (2) when the
evaluation dataset diverges significantly from the training data, indicating
the out-of-distribution scenario, or (3) when synthetic data is used in
conjunction with real images, as demonstrated in the training of CLIP models.

search_paper_list.title: EgoGen: An Egocentric Synthetic Data Generator
search_paper_list.summary:
Understanding the world in first-person view is fundamental in Augmented
Reality (AR). This immersive perspective brings dramatic visual changes and
unique challenges compared to third-person views. Synthetic data has empowered
third-person-view vision models, but its application to embodied egocentric
perception tasks remains largely unexplored. A critical challenge lies in
simulating natural human movements and behaviors that effectively steer the
embodied cameras to capture a faithful egocentric representation of the 3D
world. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoGen, a new synthetic data
generator that can produce accurate and rich ground-truth training data for
egocentric perception tasks. At the heart of EgoGen is a novel human motion
synthesis model that directly leverages egocentric visual inputs of a virtual
human to sense the 3D environment. Combined with collision-avoiding motion
primitives and a two-stage reinforcement learning approach, our motion
synthesis model offers a closed-loop solution where the embodied perception and
movement of the virtual human are seamlessly coupled. Compared to previous
works, our model eliminates the need for a pre-defined global path, and is
directly applicable to dynamic environments. Combined with our easy-to-use and
scalable data generation pipeline, we demonstrate EgoGen's efficacy in three
tasks: mapping and localization for head-mounted cameras, egocentric camera
tracking, and human mesh recovery from egocentric views. EgoGen will be fully
open-sourced, offering a practical solution for creating realistic egocentric
training data and aiming to serve as a useful tool for egocentric computer
vision research. Refer to our project page: https://ego-gen.github.io/.

search_paper_list.title: InstaGen: Enhancing Object Detection by Training on Synthetic Dataset
search_paper_list.summary:
In this paper, we present a novel paradigm to enhance the ability of object
detector, e.g., expanding categories or improving detection performance, by
training on synthetic dataset generated from diffusion models. Specifically, we
integrate an instance-level grounding head into a pre-trained, generative
diffusion model, to augment it with the ability of localising instances in the
generated images. The grounding head is trained to align the text embedding of
category names with the regional visual feature of the diffusion model, using
supervision from an off-the-shelf object detector, and a novel self-training
scheme on (novel) categories not covered by the detector. We conduct thorough
experiments to show that, this enhanced version of diffusion model, termed as
InstaGen, can serve as a data synthesizer, to enhance object detectors by
training on its generated samples, demonstrating superior performance over
existing state-of-the-art methods in open-vocabulary (+4.5 AP) and data-sparse
(+1.2 to 5.2 AP) scenarios. Project page with code:
https://fcjian.github.io/InstaGen.

search_paper_list.title: WinSyn: A High Resolution Testbed for Synthetic Data
search_paper_list.summary:
We present WinSyn, a unique dataset and testbed for creating high-quality
synthetic data with procedural modeling techniques. The dataset contains
high-resolution photographs of windows, selected from locations around the
world, with 89,318 individual window crops showcasing diverse geometric and
material characteristics. We evaluate a procedural model by training semantic
segmentation networks on both synthetic and real images and then comparing
their performances on a shared test set of real images. Specifically, we
measure the difference in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and determine the
effective number of real images to match synthetic data's training performance.
We design a baseline procedural model as a benchmark and provide 21,290
synthetically generated images. By tuning the procedural model, key factors are
identified which significantly influence the model's fidelity in replicating
real-world scenarios. Importantly, we highlight the challenge of procedural
modeling using current techniques, especially in their ability to replicate the
spatial semantics of real-world scenarios. This insight is critical because of
the potential of procedural models to bridge to hidden scene aspects such as
depth, reflectivity, material properties, and lighting conditions.

search_paper_list.title:
En3D: An Enhanced Generative Model for Sculpting 3D Humans from 2D
  Synthetic Data
search_paper_list.summary:
We present En3D, an enhanced generative scheme for sculpting high-quality 3D
human avatars. Unlike previous works that rely on scarce 3D datasets or limited
2D collections with imbalanced viewing angles and imprecise pose priors, our
approach aims to develop a zero-shot 3D generative scheme capable of producing
visually realistic, geometrically accurate and content-wise diverse 3D humans
without relying on pre-existing 3D or 2D assets. To address this challenge, we
introduce a meticulously crafted workflow that implements accurate physical
modeling to learn the enhanced 3D generative model from synthetic 2D data.
During inference, we integrate optimization modules to bridge the gap between
realistic appearances and coarse 3D shapes. Specifically, En3D comprises three
modules: a 3D generator that accurately models generalizable 3D humans with
realistic appearance from synthesized balanced, diverse, and structured human
images; a geometry sculptor that enhances shape quality using multi-view normal
constraints for intricate human anatomy; and a texturing module that
disentangles explicit texture maps with fidelity and editability, leveraging
semantical UV partitioning and a differentiable rasterizer. Experimental
results show that our approach significantly outperforms prior works in terms
of image quality, geometry accuracy and content diversity. We also showcase the
applicability of our generated avatars for animation and editing, as well as
the scalability of our approach for content-style free adaptation.

search_paper_list.title:
Portrait4D: Learning One-Shot 4D Head Avatar Synthesis using Synthetic
  Data
search_paper_list.summary:
Existing one-shot 4D head synthesis methods usually learn from monocular
videos with the aid of 3DMM reconstruction, yet the latter is evenly
challenging which restricts them from reasonable 4D head synthesis. We present
a method to learn one-shot 4D head synthesis via large-scale synthetic data.
The key is to first learn a part-wise 4D generative model from monocular images
via adversarial learning, to synthesize multi-view images of diverse identities
and full motions as training data; then leverage a transformer-based animatable
triplane reconstructor to learn 4D head reconstruction using the synthetic
data. A novel learning strategy is enforced to enhance the generalizability to
real images by disentangling the learning process of 3D reconstruction and
reenactment. Experiments demonstrate our superiority over the prior art.

search_paper_list.title:
SynFog: A Photo-realistic Synthetic Fog Dataset based on End-to-end
  Imaging Simulation for Advancing Real-World Defogging in Autonomous Driving
search_paper_list.summary:
To advance research in learning-based defogging algorithms, various synthetic
fog datasets have been developed. However, existing datasets created using the
Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM) or real-time rendering engines often
struggle to produce photo-realistic foggy images that accurately mimic the
actual imaging process. This limitation hinders the effective generalization of
models from synthetic to real data. In this paper, we introduce an end-to-end
simulation pipeline designed to generate photo-realistic foggy images. This
pipeline comprehensively considers the entire physically-based foggy scene
imaging process, closely aligning with real-world image capture methods. Based
on this pipeline, we present a new synthetic fog dataset named SynFog, which
features both sky light and active lighting conditions, as well as three levels
of fog density. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained on SynFog
exhibit superior performance in visual perception and detection accuracy
compared to others when applied to real-world foggy images.

search_paper_list.title:
MEStereo-Du2CNN: A Novel Dual Channel CNN for Learning Robust Depth
  Estimates from Multi-exposure Stereo Images for HDR 3D Applications
search_paper_list.summary:
Display technologies have evolved over the years. It is critical to develop
practical HDR capturing, processing, and display solutions to bring 3D
technologies to the next level. Depth estimation of multi-exposure stereo image
sequences is an essential task in the development of cost-effective 3D HDR
video content. In this paper, we develop a novel deep architecture for
multi-exposure stereo depth estimation. The proposed architecture has two novel
components. First, the stereo matching technique used in traditional stereo
depth estimation is revamped. For the stereo depth estimation component of our
architecture, a mono-to-stereo transfer learning approach is deployed. The
proposed formulation circumvents the cost volume construction requirement,
which is replaced by a ResNet based dual-encoder single-decoder CNN with
different weights for feature fusion. EfficientNet based blocks are used to
learn the disparity. Secondly, we combine disparity maps obtained from the
stereo images at different exposure levels using a robust disparity feature
fusion approach. The disparity maps obtained at different exposures are merged
using weight maps calculated for different quality measures. The final
predicted disparity map obtained is more robust and retains best features that
preserve the depth discontinuities. The proposed CNN offers flexibility to
train using standard dynamic range stereo data or with multi-exposure low
dynamic range stereo sequences. In terms of performance, the proposed model
surpasses state-of-the-art monocular and stereo depth estimation methods, both
quantitatively and qualitatively, on challenging Scene flow and differently
exposed Middlebury stereo datasets. The architecture performs exceedingly well
on complex natural scenes, demonstrating its usefulness for diverse 3D HDR
applications.

search_paper_list.title:
Density-guided Translator Boosts Synthetic-to-Real Unsupervised Domain
  Adaptive Segmentation of 3D Point Clouds
search_paper_list.summary:
3D synthetic-to-real unsupervised domain adaptive segmentation is crucial to
annotating new domains. Self-training is a competitive approach for this task,
but its performance is limited by different sensor sampling patterns (i.e.,
variations in point density) and incomplete training strategies. In this work,
we propose a density-guided translator (DGT), which translates point density
between domains, and integrates it into a two-stage self-training pipeline
named DGT-ST. First, in contrast to existing works that simultaneously conduct
data generation and feature/output alignment within unstable adversarial
training, we employ the non-learnable DGT to bridge the domain gap at the input
level. Second, to provide a well-initialized model for self-training, we
propose a category-level adversarial network in stage one that utilizes the
prototype to prevent negative transfer. Finally, by leveraging the designs
above, a domain-mixed self-training method with source-aware consistency loss
is proposed in stage two to narrow the domain gap further. Experiments on two
synthetic-to-real segmentation tasks (SynLiDAR $\rightarrow$ semanticKITTI and
SynLiDAR $\rightarrow$ semanticPOSS) demonstrate that DGT-ST outperforms
state-of-the-art methods, achieving 9.4$\%$ and 4.3$\%$ mIoU improvements,
respectively. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/yuan-zm/DGT-ST}.

search_paper_list.title:
Bridging the Synthetic-to-Authentic Gap: Distortion-Guided Unsupervised
  Domain Adaptation for Blind Image Quality Assessment
search_paper_list.summary:
The annotation of blind image quality assessment (BIQA) is labor-intensive
and time-consuming, especially for authentic images. Training on synthetic data
is expected to be beneficial, but synthetically trained models often suffer
from poor generalization in real domains due to domain gaps. In this work, we
make a key observation that introducing more distortion types in the synthetic
dataset may not improve or even be harmful to generalizing authentic image
quality assessment. To solve this challenge, we propose distortion-guided
unsupervised domain adaptation for BIQA (DGQA), a novel framework that
leverages adaptive multi-domain selection via prior knowledge from distortion
to match the data distribution between the source domains and the target
domain, thereby reducing negative transfer from the outlier source domains.
Extensive experiments on two cross-domain settings (synthetic distortion to
authentic distortion and synthetic distortion to algorithmic distortion) have
demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed DGQA. Besides, DGQA is
orthogonal to existing model-based BIQA methods, and can be used in combination
with such models to improve performance with less training data.

Some studies on do-main adaptation (DA) [2, 34] have shown that outlier sourcedomains that differ too much from the target domain willmay not result in performance gains or even negative trans-fers. Blind Image Quality AssessmentEarly traditional methods typically use handcrafted featuresbased on natural scene statistics [23, 24, 30]. ConclusionThe annotation of BIQA is labor-intensive and time-consuming, especially for authentic images. Training onsynthetic data is expected to be beneficial, but syntheticallytrained models often suffer from poor generalization in au-thentic distortion datasets due to domain gaps. We makea key observation that the use of a larger synthetic distor-tion dataset may not improve or even be harmful to the per-formance of model generalization to authentic distortions,and analyze the reasons for this in the context of some re-search about domain adaptation. To solve this challenge,we analyze how to measure the distance of source and tar-get domains for BIQA under unsupervised scenarios andaccordingly propose a distortion-guided unsupervised do-main adaptation framework that reduces the negative trans-fer of the outlier source domains to the target domain andimproves the generalization ability of the model. Our ap-proach significantly improves the model performance witha significantly smaller amount of training data in the set-tings of synthetic distortion to authentic distortion and syn-thetic distortion to algorithmic distortion. Besides, sinceour method is a sample-based approach, it is fully compat-ible with existing model-based approaches. Finally, we ex-plore the upper bound of the performance of the methodbased on source domain selection on KADID-10k for gen-eralizing to authentic distortion datasets and experimentallydemonstrate the feasibility of generalizing to authentic dis-tortions by generalizing over synthetic distortions.6. candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Portrait4D: Learning One-Shot 4D Head Avatar Synthesis using Synthetic
  Data
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Existing one-shot 4D head synthesis methods usually learn from monocular
videos with the aid of 3DMM reconstruction, yet the latter is evenly
challenging which restricts them from reasonable 4D head synthesis. We present
a method to learn one-shot 4D head synthesis via large-scale synthetic data.
The key is to first learn a part-wise 4D generative model from monocular images
via adversarial learning, to synthesize multi-view images of diverse identities
and full motions as training data; then leverage a transformer-based animatable
triplane reconstructor to learn 4D head reconstruction using the synthetic
data. A novel learning strategy is enforced to enhance the generalizability to
real images by disentangling the learning process of 3D reconstruction and
reenactment. Experiments demonstrate our superiority over the prior art.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a one‐shot 4D head avatar synthesis framework that produces photorealistic animatable head models with full control over facial expressions, eye gaze, head, and neck poses from a single image. The key contributions include the design of a part-wise generative head model (GenHead) for synthesizing large-scale multi-view synthetic data and a transformer-based animatable triplane reconstructor (Portrait4D) trained on this synthetic data. A disentangled learning strategy is proposed to separate static 3D reconstruction from dynamic reenactment, enhancing generalizability to real images.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach first trains a 4D generative model that leverages a tri-plane generator with part-wise deformation fields derived from FLAME mesh parameters to produce synthetic data with full motion control. This synthetic data is used to train a one-shot 4D head synthesis model that employs a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture with separate de-expression (canonicalization) and reenactment modules using cross-attention layers, self-attention layers, and volumetric rendering based on neural radiance fields. The method is trained end‐to‐end via adversarial learning with multiple supervision signals including perceptual, reconstruction, and adversarial losses.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The experiments are conducted using datasets such as FFHQ and VFHQ with images re-aligned at high resolution (e.g., 512x512). The synthetic data is generated using the proposed GenHead model, and both dynamic and static data are synthesized for training. The evaluation includes self-reenactment and cross-identity reenactment tests, quantified with metrics like LPIPS, FID, identity similarity (ID), Average Expression Distance (AED), and Average Pose Distance (APD), along with ablation studies comparing variants of the model and comparisons to state-of-the-art methods.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The method struggles with handling complex accessories, heavy makeup, and detailed textures in background regions. It can produce inferior results for nearly profile views and certain facial expressions (e.g., eye blinks) due to the reliance on synthetic data and 3DMM-based expression control. Additionally, the gap between synthetic and real data may limit performance and high-frequency details may be lost due to volume rendering resolution constraints.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research could focus on improving the quality and diversity of synthetic 4D data, incorporating real data and stronger 3D priors into an end-to-end training pipeline, extending the approach to few-shot scenarios, enhancing control over fine-grained expressions and high-frequency details, and integrating techniques (e.g., advanced deepfake detection) to prevent misuse.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title: Scaling Laws of Synthetic Images for Model Training ... for Now
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Recent significant advances in text-to-image models unlock the possibility of
training vision systems using synthetic images, potentially overcoming the
difficulty of collecting curated data at scale. It is unclear, however, how
these models behave at scale, as more synthetic data is added to the training
set. In this paper we study the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by
state of the art text-to-image models, for the training of supervised models:
image classifiers with label supervision, and CLIP with language supervision.
We identify several factors, including text prompts, classifier-free guidance
scale, and types of text-to-image models, that significantly affect scaling
behavior. After tuning these factors, we observe that synthetic images
demonstrate a scaling trend similar to, but slightly less effective than, real
images in CLIP training, while they significantly underperform in scaling when
training supervised image classifiers. Our analysis indicates that the main
reason for this underperformance is the inability of off-the-shelf
text-to-image models to generate certain concepts, a limitation that
significantly impairs the training of image classifiers. Our findings also
suggest that scaling synthetic data can be particularly effective in scenarios
such as: (1) when there is a limited supply of real images for a supervised
problem (e.g., fewer than 0.5 million images in ImageNet), (2) when the
evaluation dataset diverges significantly from the training data, indicating
the out-of-distribution scenario, or (3) when synthetic data is used in
conjunction with real images, as demonstrated in the training of CLIP models.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper presents an in-depth empirical study on the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by text-to-image models and their efficacy in training vision models. It compares the performance of models trained on synthetic data versus real data and demonstrates that while synthetic data generally underperforms in supervised ImageNet training, it can be competitive or even superior in scenarios with limited real data or OOD (out-of-distribution) settings, as well as in CLIP training.

Portrait4D: Learning One-Shot 4D Head Avatar Synthesis using Synthetic
  Data
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Existing one-shot 4D head synthesis methods usually learn from monocular
videos with the aid of 3DMM reconstruction, yet the latter is evenly
challenging which restricts them from reasonable 4D head synthesis. We present
a method to learn one-shot 4D head synthesis via large-scale synthetic data.
The key is to first learn a part-wise 4D generative model from monocular images
via adversarial learning, to synthesize multi-view images of diverse identities
and full motions as training data; then leverage a transformer-based animatable
triplane reconstructor to learn 4D head reconstruction using the synthetic
data. A novel learning strategy is enforced to enhance the generalizability to
real images by disentangling the learning process of 3D reconstruction and
reenactment. Experiments demonstrate our superiority over the prior art.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a one‐shot 4D head avatar synthesis framework that produces photorealistic animatable head models with full control over facial expressions, eye gaze, head, and neck poses from a single image. candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach first trains a 4D generative model that leverages a tri-plane generator with part-wise deformation fields derived from FLAME mesh parameters to produce synthetic data with full motion control. The method is trained end‐to‐end via adversarial learning with multiple supervision signals including perceptual, reconstruction, and adversarial losses.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The experiments are conducted using datasets such as FFHQ and VFHQ with images re-aligned at high resolution (e.g., 512x512). The synthetic data is generated using the proposed GenHead model, and both dynamic and static data are synthesized for training. candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research could focus on improving the quality and diversity of synthetic 4D data, incorporating real data and stronger 3D priors into an end-to-end training pipeline, extending the approach to few-shot scenarios, enhancing control over fine-grained expressions and high-frequency details, and integrating techniques (e.g., advanced deepfake detection) to prevent misuse.

set. In this paper we study the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by

problem (e.g., fewer than 0.5 million images in ImageNet), (2) when the
evaluation dataset diverges significantly from the training data, indicating
the out-of-distribution scenario, or (3) when synthetic data is used in
conjunction with real images, as demonstrated in the training of CLIP models.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
RealNet: A Feature Selection Network with Realistic Synthetic Anomaly
  for Anomaly Detection
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Self-supervised feature reconstruction methods have shown promising advances
in industrial image anomaly detection and localization. Despite this progress,
these methods still face challenges in synthesizing realistic and diverse
anomaly samples, as well as addressing the feature redundancy and pre-training
bias of pre-trained feature. In this work, we introduce RealNet, a feature
reconstruction network with realistic synthetic anomaly and adaptive feature
selection. It is incorporated with three key innovations: First, we propose
Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS), a diffusion
process-based synthesis strategy capable of generating samples with varying
anomaly strengths that mimic the distribution of real anomalous samples.
Second, we develop Anomaly-aware Features Selection (AFS), a method for
selecting representative and discriminative pre-trained feature subsets to
improve anomaly detection performance while controlling computational costs.
Third, we introduce Reconstruction Residuals Selection (RRS), a strategy that
adaptively selects discriminative residuals for comprehensive identification of
anomalous regions across multiple levels of granularity. We assess RealNet on
four benchmark datasets, and our results demonstrate significant improvements
in both Image AUROC and Pixel AUROC compared to the current state-o-the-art
methods. The code, data, and models are available at
https://github.com/cnulab/RealNet.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces RealNet, a novel anomaly detection framework that unifies feature reconstruction with realistic synthetic anomaly generation. Its main contributions include the development of three key components—Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS) for generating diverse and realistic synthetic anomalies, Anomaly-aware Features Selection (AFS) for selecting discriminative pre-trained feature subsets, and Reconstruction Residuals Selection (RRS) to identify key reconstruction residuals for effective anomaly scoring. The work also provides a new synthetic industrial anomaly dataset (SIA) and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: RealNet employs a self-supervised framework that first synthesizes anomalies using a diffusion process based on DDPM with an adjustable perturbation factor (SDAS). It then performs adaptive feature selection (AFS) on multi-scale pre-trained CNN features to reduce redundancy and bias. These selected features are reconstructed via dedicated networks and the difference (residuals) is processed by RRS, which selects and pools informative residuals to generate anomaly scores via a discriminator. The overall model is trained with combined reconstruction and segmentation losses.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The approach is evaluated on four benchmark datasets: MVTec-AD, MPDD, BTAD, and VisA. The experiments use metrics such as Image AUROC, Pixel AUROC, and PRO to assess detection and localization performance. A consistent backbone (WideResNet50 pre-trained on ImageNet) is employed, and ablation studies are conducted to analyze the impact of different modules (AFS, RRS) and anomaly synthesis strengths. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, as well as detailed computational efficiency analysis, are provided.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper notes that while SDAS and the synthetic anomaly dataset (SIA) perform well overall, SIA may underperform in scenarios with complex texture anomalies compared to datasets like DTD. Additionally, the diffusion-based synthesis method introduces extra offline training time (e.g., 6 hours to generate anomalies) and the design choices (e.g., using lower resolution reconstruction) can lead to minor deviations in accurately localizing small anomalous areas.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore improving synthetic texture anomaly modeling, further reducing offline training time and computational overhead, and enhancing the resolution or design of reconstruction networks to better capture small anomalies. Extending the framework to more diverse multi-class or real-world settings and refining feature selection to mitigate pre-training bias are also promising directions.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: Scaling Laws of Synthetic Images for Model Training ... for Now
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Recent significant advances in text-to-image models unlock the possibility of
training vision systems using synthetic images, potentially overcoming the
difficulty of collecting curated data at scale. It is unclear, however, how
these models behave at scale, as more synthetic data is added to the training
set. In this paper we study the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by
state of the art text-to-image models, for the training of supervised models:
image classifiers with label supervision, and CLIP with language supervision.
We identify several factors, including text prompts, classifier-free guidance
scale, and types of text-to-image models, that significantly affect scaling
behavior. After tuning these factors, we observe that synthetic images
demonstrate a scaling trend similar to, but slightly less effective than, real
images in CLIP training, while they significantly underperform in scaling when
training supervised image classifiers. Our analysis indicates that the main
reason for this underperformance is the inability of off-the-shelf
text-to-image models to generate certain concepts, a limitation that
significantly impairs the training of image classifiers. Our findings also
suggest that scaling synthetic data can be particularly effective in scenarios
such as: (1) when there is a limited supply of real images for a supervised
problem (e.g., fewer than 0.5 million images in ImageNet), (2) when the
evaluation dataset diverges significantly from the training data, indicating
the out-of-distribution scenario, or (3) when synthetic data is used in
conjunction with real images, as demonstrated in the training of CLIP models.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper investigates the scaling laws of synthetic images used for training vision models. It studies how synthetic image datasets generated by state-of-the-art text-to-image (T2I) models such as Stable Diffusion, Imagen, and Muse behave relative to real images, especially in supervised classification and CLIP training. The work reveals power-law relationships in training loss scaling, compares scaling behavior across different models and prompt configurations, and identifies classes where synthetic data may outperform real data in specific scenarios (e.g., out-of-distribution tasks).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The study leverages various T2I models using different configurations including classifier-free guidance (CFG) scales and text prompt designs (e.g., class names, descriptions, hypernyms, CLIP templates, and IN-captions) to generate large-scale synthetic image datasets. The analysis employs standard supervised training setups (using ViT-based architectures) and zero-shot training for CLIP models with extensive controlled experiments. The approach involves fitting power-law scaling curves (loss versus training set size in log space) and per-class evaluations of recognizability and diversity metrics.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on synthetic image datasets generated with different T2I models and configurations, and compared to real datasets such as ImageNet and LAION-400M. The setup includes training supervised classifiers on synthetic images (with varying dataset scales up to millions) and CLIP models for zero-shot classification over ImageNet and 15 downstream classification datasets. Validation methods include measuring cross-entropy loss, top-1 accuracy, FID, LPIPS, as well as out-of-distribution evaluations on datasets like ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The synthetic images generated by off-the-shelf T2I models do not scale as effectively as real images, particularly for supervised classification tasks on in-domain datasets, due to difficulty in accurately representing certain visual concepts. Specific classes (labeled as 'poor' in the paper) suffer from low recognizability and limited scaling ability. Additionally, the power-law scaling behavior may break down when model capacity is insufficient for very large datasets.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could focus on enhancing text-to-image models to better capture challenging concepts and improve both the recognizability and diversity of synthetic images. candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Portrait4D: Learning One-Shot 4D Head Avatar Synthesis using Synthetic
  Data
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Existing one-shot 4D head synthesis methods usually learn from monocular
videos with the aid of 3DMM reconstruction, yet the latter is evenly
challenging which restricts them from reasonable 4D head synthesis. We present
a method to learn one-shot 4D head synthesis via large-scale synthetic data.
The key is to first learn a part-wise 4D generative model from monocular images
via adversarial learning, to synthesize multi-view images of diverse identities
and full motions as training data; then leverage a transformer-based animatable
triplane reconstructor to learn 4D head reconstruction using the synthetic
data. A novel learning strategy is enforced to enhance the generalizability to
real images by disentangling the learning process of 3D reconstruction and
reenactment. Experiments demonstrate our superiority over the prior art.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a novel framework for one-shot 4D head avatar synthesis that generates photorealistic, fully controllable head avatars (including face, mouth, eyes, and neck motion) from a single monocular image. It combines a 4D generative model (GenHead) for synthesizing large-scale multi-view, motion-controlled synthetic data with a transformer-based animatable tri-plane reconstructor to achieve high-fidelity and 3D-consistent head reenactment.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach first trains a part-wise generative head model (GenHead) using adversarial learning on monocular images (e.g., from FFHQ) by leveraging a tri-plane generator with FLAME-based deformation fields to synthesize canonical head NeRF representations and full motion control. This synthetic data is then used to train a transformer-based animatable tri-plane reconstructor Ψ, which employs dual appearance encoders, a motion encoder, and a canonicalization/re-enactment module with cross-attention and self-attention layers. A novel disentangled learning strategy is used to separate static 3D reconstruction from animation, improving generalizability to real images.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The framework is evaluated using synthetic data generated from FFHQ and VFHQ datasets, and tested on self-reenactment and cross-reenactment tasks using metrics such as FID, LPIPS, identity similarity, Average Expression Distance (AED), and Average Pose Distance (APD). Ablation studies are conducted to validate the effectiveness of each component, and 3D consistency evaluations are performed.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:

  for Anomaly Detection
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:

in industrial image anomaly detection and localization. Despite this progress,
these methods still face challenges in synthesizing realistic and diverse
anomaly samples, as well as addressing the feature redundancy and pre-training
bias of pre-trained feature. In this work, we introduce RealNet, a feature
reconstruction network with realistic synthetic anomaly and adaptive feature
selection. It is incorporated with three key innovations: First, we propose
Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS), a diffusion
process-based synthesis strategy capable of generating samples with varying
anomaly strengths that mimic the distribution of real anomalous samples.
Second, we develop Anomaly-aware Features Selection (AFS), a method for
selecting representative and discriminative pre-trained feature subsets to
improve anomaly detection performance while controlling computational costs.
Third, we introduce Reconstruction Residuals Selection (RRS), a strategy that
adaptively selects discriminative residuals for comprehensive identification of
anomalous regions across multiple levels of granularity. We assess RealNet on
four benchmark datasets, and our results demonstrate significant improvements
in both Image AUROC and Pixel AUROC compared to the current state-o-the-art
methods. The code, data, and models are available at
https://github.com/cnulab/RealNet.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces RealNet, a novel anomaly detection framework that unifies feature reconstruction with realistic synthetic anomaly generation. Its main contributions include the development of three key components—Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS) for generating diverse and realistic synthetic anomalies, Anomaly-aware Features Selection (AFS) for selecting discriminative pre-trained feature subsets, and Reconstruction Residuals Selection (RRS) to identify key reconstruction residuals for effective anomaly scoring. The work also provides a new synthetic industrial anomaly dataset (SIA) and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: RealNet employs a self-supervised framework that first synthesizes anomalies using a diffusion process based on DDPM with an adjustable perturbation factor (SDAS). It then performs adaptive feature selection (AFS) on multi-scale pre-trained CNN features to reduce redundancy and bias. These selected features are reconstructed via dedicated networks and the difference (residuals) is processed by RRS, which selects and pools informative residuals to generate anomaly scores via a discriminator. The overall model is trained with combined reconstruction and segmentation losses.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The approach is evaluated on four benchmark datasets: MVTec-AD, MPDD, BTAD, and VisA. The experiments use metrics such as Image AUROC, Pixel AUROC, and PRO to assess detection and localization performance. A consistent backbone (WideResNet50 pre-trained on ImageNet) is employed, and ablation studies are conducted to analyze the impact of different modules (AFS, RRS) and anomaly synthesis strengths. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, as well as detailed computational efficiency analysis, are provided.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper notes that while SDAS and the synthetic anomaly dataset (SIA) perform well overall, SIA may underperform in scenarios with complex texture anomalies compared to datasets like DTD. candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore improving synthetic texture anomaly modeling, further reducing offline training time and computational overhead, and enhancing the resolution or design of reconstruction networks to better capture small anomalies. Portrait4D: Learning One-Shot 4D Head Avatar Synthesis using Synthetic
  Data
selected_add_paper_info_list.summary:
Existing one-shot 4D head synthesis methods usually learn from monocular
videos with the aid of 3DMM reconstruction, yet the latter is evenly
challenging which restricts them from reasonable 4D head synthesis. We present
a method to learn one-shot 4D head synthesis via large-scale synthetic data.
The key is to first learn a part-wise 4D generative model from monocular images
via adversarial learning, to synthesize multi-view images of diverse identities
and full motions as training data; then leverage a transformer-based animatable
triplane reconstructor to learn 4D head reconstruction using the synthetic
data. A novel learning strategy is enforced to enhance the generalizability to
real images by disentangling the learning process of 3D reconstruction and
reenactment. Experiments demonstrate our superiority over the prior art.
selected_add_paper_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a novel framework for one-shot 4D head avatar synthesis that leverages large-scale synthetic data to achieve photorealistic, fully animatable 3D head reconstructions. The approach addresses the limitations of traditional monocular video-based methods by avoiding unreliable 3DMM reconstructions and supports fine-grained control over facial expressions, eye gaze, and neck poses.
selected_add_paper_info_list.methodology: The method consists of two main components: a part-wise 4D generative head model (GenHead) that synthesizes multi-view, controllable head images using a tri-plane generator and deformation fields based on FLAME meshes, and a transformer-based animatable tri-plane reconstructor that reconstructs 4D head avatars from single images using a disentangled learning strategy. The reconstructor employs cross-attention modules, a pre-trained motion encoder, and a two-stage training process (dynamic and static synthetic data) to disentangle 3D reconstruction from reenactment.
selected_add_paper_info_list.experimental_setup: The framework is trained using synthetic data generated from aligned FFHQ and VFHQ datasets. The synthetic data include dynamic identities with multiple motions and camera poses, as well as static data for enhanced 3D reconstruction. Experiments are carried out via self-reenactment and cross-identity reenactment tasks using quantitative metrics such as LPIPS, FID, identity similarity, Average Expression Distance (AED), and Average Pose Distance (APD). Ablation studies and comparisons against state-of-the-art methods further validate the effectiveness of the approach.
selected_add_paper_info_list.limitations: The method may produce inferior results when processing images with heavy makeup, complex accessories, or extreme profile poses. Additionally, background reconstruction can suffer from low-frequency detail issues and texture flickering due to limitations in the 2D super-resolution module. The reliance on synthetic data and 3DMM-based parameters may also restrict motion control fidelity and cause out-of-distribution artifacts in certain cases.
selected_add_paper_info_list.future_research_directions: Potential extensions include improving the quality and diversity of synthetic 4D data, incorporating real data and stronger 3D priors into an end-to-end training framework, increasing the volume rendering resolution to capture finer details, and extending the pipeline to support few-shot head avatar synthesis for more adaptable and robust performance.

selected_add_paper_info_list.title:
Density-guided Translator Boosts Synthetic-to-Real Unsupervised Domain
  Adaptive Segmentation of 3D Point Clouds
selected_add_paper_info_list.summary:
3D synthetic-to-real unsupervised domain adaptive segmentation is crucial to
annotating new domains. Self-training is a competitive approach for this task,
but its performance is limited by different sensor sampling patterns (i.e.,
variations in point density) and incomplete training strategies. In this work,
we propose a density-guided translator (DGT), which translates point density
between domains, and integrates it into a two-stage self-training pipeline
named DGT-ST. First, in contrast to existing works that simultaneously conduct
data generation and feature/output alignment within unstable adversarial
training, we employ the non-learnable DGT to bridge the domain gap at the input
level. Second, to provide a well-initialized model for self-training, we
propose a category-level adversarial network in stage one that utilizes the
prototype to prevent negative transfer. Finally, by leveraging the designs
above, a domain-mixed self-training method with source-aware consistency loss
is proposed in stage two to narrow the domain gap further. Experiments on two
synthetic-to-real segmentation tasks (SynLiDAR $\rightarrow$ semanticKITTI and
SynLiDAR $\rightarrow$ semanticPOSS) demonstrate that DGT-ST outperforms
state-of-the-art methods, achieving 9.4$\%$ and 4.3$\%$ mIoU improvements,
respectively. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/yuan-zm/DGT-ST}.
selected_add_paper_info_list.main_contributions: The paper addresses the challenge of synthetic-to-real unsupervised domain adaptation for 3D point cloud segmentation by proposing a density-guided translator (DGT) that bridges the domain gap at the input level and a two‐stage self-training pipeline (DGT-ST). The contributions include using statistical methods to adjust point density discrepancies between synthetic and real scans and incorporating a prototype-guided category-level adversarial network (PCAN) to provide a well-initialized model for subsequent self-training with source-aware consistency via LaserMix.
selected_add_paper_info_list.methodology: The proposed approach first employs a non-learnable, statistical-based density-guided translator that partitions scans into regions and discards points based on density ratios to mimic the target domain. In stage one, a category-level adversarial network (PCAN) utilizes class prototypes to perform adaptive adversarial alignment and reduce negative transfer. In stage two, a self-training strategy is adopted using a teacher-student framework combined with LaserMix to mix scans from both domains and enforce source-aware consistency (SAC-LM) to further narrow the domain gap.
selected_add_paper_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on two synthetic-to-real UDA segmentation tasks, namely SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI and SynLiDAR to SemanticPOSS. The experiments use standard datasets and the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) metric for evaluation. Experiments are implemented in PyTorch and MinkowskiEngine using MinkUNet as the segmentation network, with extensive ablation studies performed on different components and hyperparameters, and comparisons made against state-of-the-art adversarial and self-training approaches.
selected_add_paper_info_list.limitations: Potential limitations include the dependence on a well-initialized pretrained model provided by PCAN, sensitivity to hyperparameter settings (e.g., thresholds, update frequency, smoothing coefficients), and possible challenges when sensor sampling patterns differ drastically. Additionally, while the method improves performance by modifying the point density, the impact on computational efficiency or scalability in more varied real-world scenarios is not fully addressed.
selected_add_paper_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research could explore extending the approach to handle more diverse sensor types and environmental conditions, reducing sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning, investigating alternative strategies for density translation and noise injection, integrating multi-modal data, and applying similar methodologies to other 3D tasks beyond semantic segmentation.

{"arxiv_id":"2312.04567v1","arxiv_url":"http://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04567v1","title":"Scaling Laws of Synthetic Images for Model Training ... for Now","authors":["Lijie Fan","Kaifeng Chen","Dilip Krishnan","Dina Katabi","Phillip Isola","Yonglong Tian"],"published_date":"2023-12-07T18:59:59Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"Recent significant advances in text-to-image models unlock the possibility of
training vision systems using synthetic images, potentially overcoming the
difficulty of collecting curated data at scale. It is unclear, however, how
these models behave at scale, as more synthetic data is added to the training
set. In this paper we study the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by
state of the art text-to-image models, for the training of supervised models:
image classifiers with label supervision, and CLIP with language supervision.
We identify several factors, including text prompts, classifier-free guidance
scale, and types of text-to-image models, that significantly affect scaling
behavior. After tuning these factors, we observe that synthetic images
demonstrate a scaling trend similar to, but slightly less effective than, real
images in CLIP training, while they significantly underperform in scaling when
training supervised image classifiers. Our analysis indicates that the main
reason for this underperformance is the inability of off-the-shelf
text-to-image models to generate certain concepts, a limitation that
significantly impairs the training of image classifiers. Our findings also
suggest that scaling synthetic data can be particularly effective in scenarios
such as: (1) when there is a limited supply of real images for a supervised
problem (e.g., fewer than 0.5 million images in ImageNet), (2) when the
evaluation dataset diverges significantly from the training data, indicating
the out-of-distribution scenario, or (3) when synthetic data is used in
conjunction with real images, as demonstrated in the training of CLIP models.","github_url":"https://github.com/openai/CLIP","main_contributions":"The paper presents an in-depth empirical study on the scaling laws of synthetic images generated by text-to-image models and their efficacy in training vision models. It compares the performance of models trained on synthetic data versus real data and demonstrates that while synthetic data generally underperforms in supervised ImageNet training, it can be competitive or even superior in scenarios with limited real data or OOD (out-of-distribution) settings, as well as in CLIP training.","methodology":"The authors generate synthetic images using state-of-the-art text-to-image models (Stable Diffusion, Imagen, and Muse) with various prompt configurations and classifier-free guidance scales. These images are then used to train supervised classifiers (using ViT-B and ViT-L backbones) and CLIP models, with performance analyzed via power-law scaling of training loss versus dataset size, recognizability and diversity metrics, and zero-shot evaluation on downstream datasets.","experimental_setup":"Experiments were conducted on synthetic ImageNet datasets (using 1.3M images in different configurations), real ImageNet, and large-scale datasets like LAION-400M for CLIP training. The study evaluated models on standard benchmarks including ImageNet validation, as well as OOD datasets like ImageNet-A, -R, -Sketch, and ImageNet-V2, plus 15 downstream classification tasks (e.g., Food-101, CIFAR-10, SUN397, Cars, Aircraft) using metrics such as top-1 accuracy, cross-entropy losses, and zero-shot transfer performance.","limitations":"The study finds that synthetic images have limited scaling ability compared to real images, particularly in supervised classification tasks. The text-to-image models struggle with certain challenging or "poor" classes due to limitations in accurately generating the intended concepts, resulting in a trade-off between image diversity and recognizability.","future_research_directions":"Future work could focus on improving text-to-image models to better capture complex or challenging classes, enhancing prompt engineering and CFG parameter tuning to balance diversity and accuracy, developing more task-specific metrics for evaluating synthetic data, and exploring more effective integration of synthetic and real images to boost performance, especially in low-data or out-of-distribution scenarios."}

{"arxiv_id":"2403.05897v1","arxiv_url":"http://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05897v1","title":"RealNet: A Feature Selection Network with Realistic Synthetic Anomaly
  for Anomaly Detection","authors":["Ximiao Zhang","Min Xu","Xiuzhuang Zhou"],"published_date":"2024-03-09T12:25:01Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"Self-supervised feature reconstruction methods have shown promising advances
in industrial image anomaly detection and localization. Despite this progress,
these methods still face challenges in synthesizing realistic and diverse
anomaly samples, as well as addressing the feature redundancy and pre-training
bias of pre-trained feature. In this work, we introduce RealNet, a feature
reconstruction network with realistic synthetic anomaly and adaptive feature
selection. It is incorporated with three key innovations: First, we propose
Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS), a diffusion
process-based synthesis strategy capable of generating samples with varying
anomaly strengths that mimic the distribution of real anomalous samples.
Second, we develop Anomaly-aware Features Selection (AFS), a method for
selecting representative and discriminative pre-trained feature subsets to
improve anomaly detection performance while controlling computational costs.
Third, we introduce Reconstruction Residuals Selection (RRS), a strategy that
adaptively selects discriminative residuals for comprehensive identification of
anomalous regions across multiple levels of granularity. We assess RealNet on
four benchmark datasets, and our results demonstrate significant improvements
in both Image AUROC and Pixel AUROC compared to the current state-o-the-art
methods. The code, data, and models are available at
https://github.com/cnulab/RealNet.","github_url":"https://github.com/cnulab/RealNet","main_contributions":"The paper introduces RealNet, a novel anomaly detection framework that unifies feature reconstruction with realistic synthetic anomaly generation. Its main contributions include the development of three key components—Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS) for generating diverse and realistic synthetic anomalies, Anomaly-aware Features Selection (AFS) for selecting discriminative pre-trained feature subsets, and Reconstruction Residuals Selection (RRS) to identify key reconstruction residuals for effective anomaly scoring. The work also provides a new synthetic industrial anomaly dataset (SIA) and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.","methodology":"RealNet employs a self-supervised framework that first synthesizes anomalies using a diffusion process based on DDPM with an adjustable perturbation factor (SDAS). It then performs adaptive feature selection (AFS) on multi-scale pre-trained CNN features to reduce redundancy and bias. These selected features are reconstructed via dedicated networks and the difference (residuals) is processed by RRS, which selects and pools informative residuals to generate anomaly scores via a discriminator. The overall model is trained with combined reconstruction and segmentation losses.","experimental_setup":"The approach is evaluated on four benchmark datasets: MVTec-AD, MPDD, BTAD, and VisA. The experiments use metrics such as Image AUROC, Pixel AUROC, and PRO to assess detection and localization performance. A consistent backbone (WideResNet50 pre-trained on ImageNet) is employed, and ablation studies are conducted to analyze the impact of different modules (AFS, RRS) and anomaly synthesis strengths. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, as well as detailed computational efficiency analysis, are provided.","limitations":"The paper notes that while SDAS and the synthetic anomaly dataset (SIA) perform well overall, SIA may underperform in scenarios with complex texture anomalies compared to datasets like DTD. Additionally, the diffusion-based synthesis method introduces extra offline training time (e.g., 6 hours to generate anomalies) and the design choices (e.g., using lower resolution reconstruction) can lead to minor deviations in accurately localizing small anomalous areas.","future_research_directions":"Future work could explore improving synthetic texture anomaly modeling, further reducing offline training time and computational overhead, and enhancing the resolution or design of reconstruction networks to better capture small anomalies. Extending the framework to more diverse multi-class or real-world settings and refining feature selection to mitigate pre-training bias are also promising directions."}

new_method:
Below is the outcome of step 3—a genuinely new method that combines insights from the Base Method with ideas drawn from one of the Add Methods:

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Diffusion-Enhanced Concept Augmentation (DECA)

Overview:
The Base Method shows that synthetic images generated by text-to-image models suffer when training supervised classifiers—primarily because these models struggle to capture certain challenging or underrepresented visual concepts. In contrast, RealNet’s Strength-controllable Diffusion Anomaly Synthesis (SDAS) demonstrates how a diffusion process tuned with a controllable strength parameter can generate realistic variations. DECA merges these insights by introducing a diffusion-based augmentation stage that selectively “boosts” the synthetic dataset with enhanced detail for underrepresented visual concepts.

Key Steps:

1. Identification of Underperforming Classes:
 • Run an initial analysis—using a small held-out validation set or a teacher classifier—to determine which classes produced by the text-to-image model are failing to capture key attributes or suffer from low recognizability.
 • Compute feature discrepancy metrics (e.g., differences in key embedding distributions) between synthetic samples of each class and available real-world prototypes to quantitatively flag “weak” classes.

2. Prototype-Guided Diffusion Conditioning:
 • For each underperforming class, extract a set of representative concept “prototypes” (these could be manually selected real examples or synthesized “ideal” features obtained via a feature extractor).
 • Feed these prototypes, together with the original class text prompts, into a controllable diffusion model. The diffusion process is conditioned not only on the text but also on the visual cues from the prototypes.
 • Use a tunable strength parameter that adjusts how strongly the generated sample should align with these prototypes. In effect, the diffusion model “injects” missing visual details (or even subtle anomalies that boost class diversity) into the synthesized image.

3. Diffusion-Based Augmented Data Generation:
 • For each flagged underperforming class, augment the original synthetic dataset by generating a suite of diffusion-enhanced images that cover a spectrum of the diffusion strength—from mild enhancements (preserving global diversity) to strong detail injection (boosting scarce semantic details).
 • Optionally, apply an automatic filtering stage (using pre-trained feature extractors) to ensure that only those images that reduce the discrepancy with real prototypes are retained.

4. Composite Training Dataset Construction:
 • Merge the diffusion-augmented images with the baseline synthetic images generated by the text-to-image model.
 • Use domain mixing strategies (e.g., curriculum learning or adaptive sampling based on class difficulty) so that the classifier sees both generations, emphasizing the diffusion-enhanced data for classes that initially underperformed.

5. End-to-End Training with Feedback Loop:
 • Train the downstream classifier on this composite dataset.
 • Incorporate a feedback loop where periodic evaluation of class performance directs further fine-tuning of the diffusion strength parameters and the selection criteria for augmented images.

Expected Benefits:
 • Enhanced visual fidelity for challenging concepts—by “filling in” missing details that were absent in the baseline generation.
 • Improved scaling behavior for supervised classifiers, reducing the gap between synthetic and real image performance.
 • Greater intra-class diversity without sacrificing recognizability, thanks to controlled synthesis dynamics inherited from the diffusion model.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
This method, Diffusion-Enhanced Concept Augmentation (DECA), goes well beyond a partial modification of the Base Method. By embedding a controllable diffusion augmentation stage that is conditioned on class-specific visual prototypes, DECA actively addresses the known failure modes of standard text-to-image synthesis when training supervised image classifiers.
verification_policy:
Below is an outline of three concrete experiments, all of which can be implemented in Python using common deep learning libraries (e.g., PyTorch, TensorFlow) and off‐the‐shelf diffusion models. Each experiment is designed to highlight a different aspect of the superiority of the DECA method while staying within realistic coding tasks.

─────────────────────────────  
1. Experiment: Evaluating Classification Performance with Diffusion-Augmented Data

Objective:
 • Compare the downstream classifier’s accuracy when trained on (a) the baseline synthetic dataset produced by the text-to-image model versus (b) a composite dataset that includes diffusion-enhanced images for the underperforming classes.

Plan:
 – Run the Base Method to generate synthetic images for all classes.
 – Identify “weak” classes using a small held-out dataset or a teacher classifier (this can be achieved by comparing classification scores or embedding discrepancies computed via a pre-trained feature extractor).
 – For each weak class, apply the DECA augmentation stage to generate several images per class using a diffusion model conditioned on both the original prompt and a set of real-prototype images.
 – Merge the original synthetic images with the diffusion-augmented ones using a domain-mixing strategy (possibly via adaptive sampling weights).
 – Train a supervised classifier (e.g., using a standard CNN or ResNet architecture) on each dataset variant.
 – Report metrics such as overall accuracy, per-class accuracy, and confusion matrices to show improvements.

Implementation Hint (Python/PyTorch pseudocode):

------------------------------------------------

    enhanced_img = diffusion_model.generate(prompt, conditioning_images=prototypes, strength=strength)
    return enhanced_img

# (4) Construct composite dataset and prepare PyTorch dataloaders

# (5) Define, train and evaluate a CNN classifier
model = models.resnet18(pretrained=False)
# ... training loop ...
------------------------------------------------

─────────────────────────────  
2. Experiment: Ablation Study on Diffusion Strength Parameter

Objective:
 • Assess the effect of the diffusion strength parameter on the quality of the augmented images. Show that tuning this strength parameter helps reduce the discrepancy between synthetic and real prototypes.

Plan:
 – For a fixed underperforming class, sample a set of prototype images from the real dataset.
 – Vary the diffusion strength parameter across a range (e.g., low, medium, high).
 – For each parameter setting, generate images using the DECA process.
 – Calculate a quantitative metric such as the feature discrepancy (e.g., using Euclidean distance or cosine similarity between embeddings from a pre-trained feature extractor like VGG/ResNet) between the generated images and the real prototypes.
 – Plot the discrepancy metric as a function of the diffusion strength to find the optimal boosting level.

Below is a detailed experimental plan with three distinct experiments that follow the verification policy. Each experiment is explained with its objective, step‐by‐step procedure, and sample Python/PyTorch code snippets. These experiments are designed to verify different claims of the DECA method. In all experiments we assume that a text-to-image synthesis model and a diffusion model (with an API allowing both text and visual conditioning) are available as off‐the‐shelf. We also assume that existing PyTorch libraries (torchvision, numpy, matplotlib, etc.) are used as much as possible.

Experiment 1: Evaluating Classification Performance with Diffusion-Augmented Data

Objective:
 • To compare the downstream classifier’s accuracy by training on (a) a full synthetic dataset generated by a text-to-image model (baseline) versus (b) a composite dataset where “weak” (or underperforming) classes have been enhanced by applying the diffusion augmentation process (DECA).

Steps:
1. Generate a baseline synthetic dataset:
 – Use a text-to-image model to generate synthetic images for all classes.
 – Organize the images and labels into a dataset; split into training and validation sets.
2. Identify underperforming (“weak”) classes:
 – Use a small held-out real dataset or a teacher classifier to evaluate a pretrained feature extractor’s output.
 – Compare features (e.g., via Euclidean or cosine distances) between synthetic images and corresponding real-prototype images.
3. For the weak classes, generate diffusion-enhanced images:
 – Call the diffusion model API using both the original text prompt and additional real prototype images for conditioning.
 – Generate several diffusion-augmented images for each weak class.
4. Construct the composite dataset:
 – Merge the baseline synthetic images with the new diffusion-enhanced images, applying a domain-mixing strategy (the simplest is to use fixed or adaptive sampling weights).
5. Train a classifier on both datasets:
 – Use a common CNN architecture (for example, ResNet18) for training.
 – Evaluate the final performance using overall accuracy, per-class accuracy, and confusion matrices.

Experiment 2: Ablation Study on Diffusion Strength Parameter

Objective:
 • To quantitatively analyze the effect of the diffusion strength parameter on the quality of augmented images. The goal is to find the optimum strength that minimizes feature discrepancies (between generated images and real prototypes).

Steps:
1. Select a single underperforming class (for example, one from the weak_classes identified earlier) and sample a fixed set of real prototype images.
2. Define a range of diffusion strength values (e.g., [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]).
3. For each strength value, generate multiple images through the DECA process.
4. Use a pretrained feature extractor (e.g., ResNet18 or VGG) to extract image embeddings from both the generated images and their corresponding prototypes.
5. Compute the discrepancy using a metric (for example, the Euclidean distance or cosine similarity).
6. Plot the relationship between the diffusion strength and the computed feature discrepancy to identify an optimal value.

Experiment 3: Impact of Domain Mixing Strategies via Curriculum Learning

Objective:
 • To evaluate whether an adaptive domain mixing strategy (via curriculum learning) leads to improved convergence and overall classifier performance compared to a static, fixed mixing ratio between baseline synthetic images and diffusion-enhanced images.

Steps:
1. Prepare two training regimes:
 a) Static Mixing – Where the synthetic dataset and diffusion-enhanced images are merged with a fixed ratio.
 b) Adaptive (Curriculum) Mixing – Start training with a higher proportion of synthetic images and gradually increase the portion of diffusion-enhanced images through adaptive sampling as training progresses.
2. Train identical neural network classifiers under both regimes.
3. Monitor training convergence by tracking loss curves and validation accuracy over epochs, and finally compare overall classification accuracy.

Below is the pseudocode for the adaptive curriculum approach that adjusts the mixing ratio over epochs:

------------------------------------------------
import numpy as np

# Assume baseline_loader and diffusion_loader are PyTorch DataLoaders defined for synthetic and diffusion-enhanced images respectively

def get_mixed_batch(epoch, total_epochs, batch_baseline, batch_diffused):
    # Curriculum mixing: gradually increase probability of sampling from diffusion-enhanced images
    ratio = epoch / total_epochs  # goes from 0 (only baseline) to 1 (only diffused)
    mixed_batch = []
    # Ensure both batches are of same size (or use zip with min length)
    for b_sample, d_sample in zip(batch_baseline, batch_diffused):
        # For each pair, choose the diffusion-enhanced sample with probability = ratio
        mixed_batch.append(d_sample if np.random.rand() < ratio else b_sample)
    return torch.stack(mixed_batch)

# Define training loop with curriculum learning
total_epochs = 20
model = models.resnet18(pretrained=False, num_classes=len(class_prompts))
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

def train_with_curriculum(model, baseline_loader, diffusion_loader, total_epochs):
    model.train()
    for epoch in range(total_epochs):
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        for (images_b, labels_b), (images_d, labels_d) in zip(baseline_loader, diffusion_loader):
            # Get mixed batch using the current epoch ratio
            mixed_images = get_mixed_batch(epoch, total_epochs, images_b, images_d)
            
            # For labels, assume a similar mixing strategy; here simply choose baseline labels unless diffusion labels are critical.
            # In practice, one might also mix labels accordingly.
            mixed_labels = labels_b  # or combine accordingly
            
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(mixed_images)
            loss = criterion(outputs, mixed_labels)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            epoch_loss += loss.item()
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{total_epochs}, Loss: {epoch_loss:.4f}")
    return model

# Training with static mixing can be implemented by simply concatenating the two datasets with a fixed ratio.
# For brevity, we focus on the adaptive curriculum training.

        return Image.fromarray(array)

class DummyDiffusionModel:
    # Simulate a diffusion model that “enhances” a generated image by applying slight modifications.
    def generate(self, prompt, conditioning_images=None, strength=0.5, size=(64, 64)):
        # For demonstration, we generate a base image and then “enhance” by blurring
        base = np.uint8(255 * np.random.rand(size[0], size[1], 3))
        img = Image.fromarray(base)
        # Conditioning: if provided, average the image with a random prototype
        if conditioning_images is not None and len(conditioning_images) > 0:
            proto = conditioning_images[random.randint(0, len(conditioning_images)-1)]
            proto = proto.resize(size)
            base_proto = np.array(proto, dtype=np.float32)
            base_img = np.array(img, dtype=np.float32)
            combined = (1-strength)*base_img + strength*base_proto
            combined = np.clip(combined, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
            img = Image.fromarray(combined)
        # Further simulate diffusion “enhancement” with a mild blur that increases with strength.
        blur_radius = strength * 2.0  # adjust scale as needed
        img = img.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(radius=blur_radius))
        return img

    for idx, prompt in enumerate(class_prompts):
        if idx in weak_classes:
            real_protos = load_real_prototype_images(num_classes=num_classes, per_class=5)[idx]
            for _ in range(50):
                img = diffusion_model.generate(prompt, conditioning_images=real_protos, strength=0.7)
                diffusion_images.append(img)
                diffusion_labels.append(idx)
    diffusion_dataset = MyCustomImageDataset(diffusion_images, diffusion_labels, transform=transform)
    diffusion_loader = DataLoader(diffusion_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    model = models.resnet18(pretrained=False, num_classes=num_classes).to(device)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    total_epochs = 5  # using fewer epochs for demonstration

    # Function to get a mixed batch from two batches using curriculum mixing.
    def get_mixed_batch(epoch, total_epochs, batch_baseline, batch_diffused):
        ratio = epoch / total_epochs  # between 0 and 1; increases over epochs
        mixed_images = []
        mixed_labels = []
        # Ensure equal length by taking the minimum.
        min_len = min(len(batch_baseline[0]), len(batch_diffused[0]))
        for i in range(min_len):
            # With probability = ratio, sample from diffusion batch; otherwise baseline.
            if random.random() < ratio:
                mixed_images.append(batch_diffused[0][i])
                mixed_labels.append(batch_diffused[1][i])
            else:
                mixed_images.append(batch_baseline[0][i])
                mixed_labels.append(batch_baseline[1][i])
        mixed_images = torch.stack(mixed_images)
        mixed_labels = torch.tensor(mixed_labels)
        return mixed_images.to(device), mixed_labels.to(device)

    # Training with adaptive (curriculum) domain mixing
    loss_history = []
    print("Starting training with adaptive (curriculum) mixing strategy...")
    for epoch in range(1, total_epochs+1):
        model.train()
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        # Use zip to iterate over both loaders (taking min batches)
        for (images_b, labels_b), (images_d, labels_d) in zip(baseline_loader, diffusion_loader):
            mixed_images, mixed_labels = get_mixed_batch(epoch, total_epochs, (images_b, labels_b), (images_d, labels_d))
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(mixed_images)
            loss = criterion(outputs, mixed_labels)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            epoch_loss += loss.item()
        avg_epoch_loss = epoch_loss / len(baseline_loader)
        loss_history.append(avg_epoch_loss)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch}/{total_epochs} - Loss: {avg_epoch_loss:.4f}")

    # Plot the curriculum training loss curve
    epochs = range(1, total_epochs+1)
    plt.figure()
    plt.plot(epochs, loss_history, marker='o')
    plt.xlabel('Epoch')
    plt.ylabel('Loss')
    plt.title('Curriculum Training Loss (Adaptive Domain Mixing)')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("training_loss_curriculum.pdf")
    plt.close()
    print("Saved curriculum training loss plot as 'training_loss_curriculum.pdf'.")
    print("\nExperiment 3 completed.\n")
